scenarios.title: The urgent invoice
scenarios.situation: You receive an email from your CEO's exact display name: 'Urgent: wire $48,000 to this vendor today, details attached. Don't call, I'm in meetings.' The sending address is ceo-name@company-support.co, not your company domain.
choices: Do not act on the email; verify the request through a separate trusted channel before doing anything
Wire the money quickly since the CEO said it is urgent and marked don't call
Reply asking for confirmation, since a reply proves the address is real
Forward it to finance so they can decide
scenarios.why: This is a business email compromise pattern: display-name spoofing plus urgency plus a no-call instruction. Replying or forwarding keeps you inside the attacker's channel. Verification must happen out-of-band (known phone number, in person, internal chat) because anything in the email thread is attacker-controlled.
scenarios.hint: Which parts of this email could an attacker fake, and which channel could they not fake?

scenarios.title: The open bucket
scenarios.situation: A teammate shares a link to a cloud storage bucket containing customer exports 'for quick access.' The link works in a private browser window with no login. The bucket holds 40,000 customer records.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct immediate response?
choices: Treat it as an active exposure: restrict the bucket to private immediately, then assess who may have accessed it
Bookmark the link since it is convenient for the team
Email the link to the team so everyone can use it before it is fixed
Do nothing; the URL is long and unguessable so it is effectively private
scenarios.why: An unauthenticated URL to sensitive data is a public exposure regardless of URL length: links leak through logs, referers, and forwards. The first move is always containment (make it private), then forensics (access logs), then process (why was customer data exported to a shared bucket at all).
scenarios.hint: How many ways can a 'secret' URL escape that you would never know about?

scenarios.title: The midnight logins
scenarios.situation: The authentication logs show 400 failed logins for one service account in the last hour, from IP addresses in six countries. The account has never logged in from outside your office network before.
scenarios.prompt: What does this indicate and what is the first action?
evidence: auth.log (sample)

02:11 fail svc-backup from 91.203.x.x
02:14 fail svc-backup from 45.155.x.x
02:31 fail svc-backup from 185.220.x.x
... 397 more
choices: A distributed password-guessing attack; lock or rotate the account credentials and block the source IPs at the perimeter
Normal background noise; service accounts get probed constantly and the failures prove the password held
A misconfigured internal script; restart the backup service
Evidence of a successful breach; wipe the server immediately
scenarios.why: Hundreds of failures across many source IPs is the signature of a distributed brute-force or credential-stuffing attack, and rotation to distributed sources is meant to dodge per-IP rate limits. The failures only prove the password held so far; the account must be locked/rotated and the IPs blocked before one guess lands. Wiping destroys evidence before you know the scope.
scenarios.hint: Why would an attacker use six countries instead of one machine?

scenarios.title: Patch versus ship
scenarios.situation: A critical vulnerability is announced in a library you use in production. The vendor patch requires a minor version bump with 'possible behavior changes.' Your team ships a major customer release in four days, and the release branch is frozen.
choices: Assess exploitability first: if the vulnerable code path is reachable in your deployment, patch now (even on the frozen branch); if not, schedule the patch immediately after release with a documented risk acceptance
Always wait until after the release; frozen means frozen
Always patch immediately regardless of reachability; security beats schedule
Remove the library entirely to eliminate the risk
scenarios.why: Not every CVE is exploitable in your deployment: the risk decision hinges on whether the vulnerable code path is reachable and exposed. Patching blindly on a frozen branch risks breaking the release; waiting blindly risks breach. The professional move is a fast exploitability assessment, then patch-now or documented risk-acceptance with a hard date.
scenarios.hint: What two facts determine whether this vulnerability can actually hurt you?

scenarios.title: Contain or clean
scenarios.situation: You confirm an attacker has an active session on a production server. They appear to still be exploring. Your backups are tested and current. The team wants to immediately wipe and rebuild the server.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct incident-response order?
choices: Contain first (isolate the host from the network while preserving its state), capture forensic evidence, then eradicate and rebuild from known-good media
Wipe and rebuild immediately to cut off the attacker as fast as possible
Watch the attacker silently to learn their full toolkit before acting
Reboot the server, which will drop the attacker's session
scenarios.why: The standard order is contain, eradicate, recover: isolate the host so the attacker cannot move laterally or exfiltrate, while preserving memory and disk for forensics. Wiping first destroys evidence of how they got in, which means you will rebuild a still-vulnerable system. Watching an active intruder risks data theft for uncertain intelligence value.
scenarios.hint: What do you lose forever the moment you wipe, and what does the attacker gain every minute you wait?

scenarios.title: The vendor breach
scenarios.situation: A SaaS vendor that holds your customer support tickets discloses a breach: attackers accessed their systems for three weeks. Your API keys for their service are stored in your secrets manager, and your team used the vendor's SSO integration.
choices: Rotate all credentials and tokens shared with the vendor, review what data of yours they held and notify affected parties per your obligations, and reassess the vendor relationship
Do nothing until the vendor publishes full details; acting early might be unnecessary
Only rotate the API keys, since SSO means the attacker could not reach your systems
Immediately terminate the vendor contract and migrate off the platform this week
scenarios.why: A vendor breach is a supply-chain incident: assume any credential, token, or session shared with the vendor is compromised and rotate it. SSO does not save you if the attacker harvested tokens or session material from the vendor side. You also inherit notification obligations for your customers' data. Terminating the contract mid-crisis is theater; assess first.
scenarios.hint: What did you hand to this vendor that an attacker inside their systems could now hold?

lessons.title: Cyber — Core concepts
concepts: The CIA triad frames every control: confidentiality (only the right eyes), integrity (data unaltered), availability (there when needed). Every incident damages at least one.
Think in attack surface: every open port, exposed bucket, and third-party integration is a door. Inventory yours before an attacker does.
Defense in depth means no single control is trusted alone: patching, least privilege, network segmentation, logging, and backups overlap so one failure is not fatal.
Offense informs defense: understanding phishing, brute force, and lateral movement tells you which logs to watch and which controls actually matter.
Least privilege is a habit, not a project: every account, key, and token should hold the minimum access it needs, and credentials shared with vendors are compromise candidates by default.
Governance turns practice into policy: risk assessments, documented acceptances, and tested backups are what make security repeatable instead of heroic.

example.walkthrough: List every listening socket not bound to localhost: each line is attack surface. Port 8080 open to the world should have a name, an owner, and a reason; anything you cannot explain gets investigated or closed.

pitfalls: Common trap: security by obscurity; an unguessable URL or hidden port is not access control.
Common trap: default credentials on internal tools ('it is only on the LAN') that become reachable after one network change.
Common trap: untested backups; a backup you have never restored is a hope, not a control.
Common trap: patching everything immediately without assessing exploitability, which breaks releases for theoretical risk.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Harden a fresh server checklist
labs.objective: Apply baseline hardening to a new Linux host: updates, firewall, and key-only SSH.
steps: List all user accounts and flag any without a clear owner.
Enable the host firewall and allow only SSH and required service ports.
Disable password authentication in sshd_config and require key-based login.
Confirm no unexpected listening services remain with ss -tlnp.
Record every change in hardening-log.txt with a timestamp.

checks.hint: Verify SSH is the only world-listening service left.
Check sshd_config shows password authentication disabled.

labs.title: Triage suspicious auth logs
labs.objective: Detect a brute-force pattern in auth logs and summarize the attack.
steps: Extract all 'Failed password' lines from auth.log for the last 24 hours.
Count failures per source IP and sort descending.
Count distinct source IPs targeting the same account.
Identify the top targeted account and its failure count.
Write a one-paragraph incident summary to triage.txt with recommended actions.

checks.hint: Filter the log for failed authentication lines first.
Your summary should end with recommended actions.

simulations.title: The 2 AM phishing report
simulations.brief: 2:14 AM. The on-call phone buzzes: a finance analyst clicked a link in an email that 'looked like IT'. Work the incident the way a real SOC would — verify first, contain second, learn third.

steps.symptom: Analyst: 'I clicked the link. It asked for my login and I typed it in. Is that bad?'
evidence: Ticket #2214

PHISHING REPORT — user: finance-analyst-02
Clicked link in 'IT password expiry' email | entered credentials
Host: FIN-1042
options: Wipe FIN-1042 immediately — scorched earth, questions later
Verify the email is actually malicious (check the link destination and sender), and force a password reset plus session revocation right away
Tell the analyst it is probably fine and close the ticket
Forward the email to the whole company as a warning
steps.explain: Verify before you escalate — checking the link destination and sender separates a drill from a breach. But entered credentials are live ammunition: the password dies NOW and the attacker's sessions get revoked with it. Wiping first destroys evidence; dismissing destroys trust.

steps.symptom: The link went to a lookalike domain registered yesterday. The credentials are compromised.
evidence: Verification

Link destination: it-helpdesk-secure[.]net (registered 2026-10-07)
Sender: spoofed internal display name, external envelope
Verdict: credential-harvesting phish
options: Reset the analyst's password and revoke all active sessions
Only reset the password — sessions expire on their own
Block the domain and call it done
Ask the analyst to change the password themselves next week
steps.explain: A harvested password stays dangerous until the reset lands AND the attacker's sessions are killed. Session revocation is the step people forget — a reset alone leaves the attacker's already-logged-in session working.

steps.symptom: Contained. Now: three other people received the same email.
evidence: Blast radius

Same campaign delivered to 4 mailboxes
1 clicked, 3 unopened
options: Purge the campaign from all mailboxes and give the three recipients a 60-second briefing
Do nothing — they did not click
Name and shame the analyst in the team channel so others learn
Block all external email company-wide
steps.explain: Unexpired threats get removed from every mailbox, and the three recipients get a short briefing while the lesson is fresh. Blame creates silence — the next person who clicks will hide it instead of reporting it.

simulations.debrief: You verified before panicking, killed the compromised credentials and sessions, swept the campaign from every mailbox, and kept the reporter as an ally. That is the defensive loop: detect, verify, contain, learn.

simulations.title: Isolate or observe?
simulations.brief: EDR flags a developer laptop: a new process is beaconing to an unknown IP every 60 seconds. The developer is mid-demo for a client. Isolate the host now, or watch and gather intelligence? There is no free choice — pick, and own it.

steps.symptom: Beaconing detected: 60-second intervals to an unknown external IP. The laptop's owner presents to a client in 20 minutes.
evidence: EDR alert

ALERT-8812 | host: DEV-2207 | process: updater-svc.exe (unsigned)
Beacon: 60s interval -> 185.220.101.4 | first seen 40 min ago
User: client demo at 10:00
options: Isolate the host now — kill the demo if you have to
Let the demo finish, then isolate — 20 minutes will not matter
Watch silently and collect a full packet capture first
Remote-wipe the laptop immediately
steps.explain: A 60-second beacon to an unknown IP from an unsigned binary is active compromise until proven otherwise. Twenty more minutes of beaconing is twenty minutes of exfiltration. You can explain a dead demo; you cannot un-exfiltrate source code.

steps.symptom: Host isolated. Forensics: the 'updater' was a trojanized build tool downloaded from a forum. It exfiltrated 40 MB before isolation.
evidence: Forensics

updater-svc.exe: trojanized toolchain, downloaded from a forum link
Exfiltrated ~40 MB before isolation | contained to DEV-2207
options: Rotate the developer's credentials, scope what the 40 MB touched, and brief the team honestly
Reimage and move on — 40 MB is nothing
Escalate to fire the developer for downloading from a forum
Keep it quiet to avoid alarming the client
steps.explain: Isolation stops the bleeding; it does not undo it. You scope what left the building, rotate everything the host touched, and tell the team the true story — quiet cover-ups are how the next incident starts.

steps.symptom: The client asks why the demo died mid-call.
evidence: Comms
Client: 'Your engineer just vanished from the call. Is everything alright?'
options: 'We detected a security event and contained it — the demo is rescheduled, and your data was not involved'
Say it was technical difficulties
Give the client the full forensic detail
Blame the developer by name
steps.explain: Honest, bounded, professional: name the category (security event), the action (contained), the impact boundary (their data not involved), and the next step (reschedule). Clients respect containment; they punish discovered lies.

simulations.debrief: You chose containment over comfort, scoped the real damage instead of hoping, and communicated honestly with the client. Incident response is a series of uncomfortable right calls — this was three of them.

simulations.title: The shared admin password
simulations.brief: During a routine review you find it: one admin password, shared by six people, unchanged in two years, sitting in a chat channel. Nobody 'owns' it. Respond like the adult in the room.

steps.symptom: The shared credential is confirmed: six users, one password, posted in a chat channel two years ago.
evidence: Finding

Account: svc-admin | shared by 6 engineers
Last rotated: 2024 (never) | location: #ops-general chat history
Scope: production database + hypervisor console
options: Rotate the password immediately, then tell everyone the new value in the same chat
Rotate the password immediately into a vault, issue individual accounts, and retire the shared one
Leave it — changing it might break someone's workflow
Email the password to all six people so everyone has the new one
steps.explain: Rotate first, because every hour it lives is another hour of un-attributable access. But the new secret goes in a vault with individual accounts — replacing one shared password with another just resets the clock on the same problem.

steps.symptom: The password is rotated and vaulted. Two engineers complain the new individual logins are 'slower'.
evidence: Feedback

eng-03: 'It takes me 30 extra seconds to check out the credential.'
eng-05: 'Can we just get the old one back for emergencies?'
options: Restore the shared password for emergencies
Hold the line, explain that attribution is the point, and streamline the vault checkout flow
Exempt senior engineers from the new process
Stop talking about it and hope the complaints fade
steps.explain: Friction complaints are real — so you reduce the friction (faster vault checkout, SSO) instead of restoring the risk. The moment you carve out exceptions, the shared-password culture is back with extra steps.

steps.symptom: Now you must make sure this does not happen again.
evidence: Goal
Prevent the next shared credential from living two years in a chat channel
options: Run a one-time scan for secrets in chat history and add a recurring secret-scan to the pipeline
Send a reminder email about password policy
Punish whoever posted it originally
Ban chat channels
steps.explain: Culture follows tooling: an automated secret-scan that catches the next one on day one beats a policy email everyone forgets by Friday. Detect the pattern, not the person.

simulations.debrief: You rotated without re-sharing, held the line on individual accountability while reducing friction, and built detection instead of blame. That is how a shared-password culture actually dies.

simulations.title: Patch Tuesday standoff
simulations.brief: A critical remote-code-execution flaw drops at noon. One internet-facing server is vulnerable — and there is a change freeze for tomorrow's product launch. Patch now and risk the launch, or hold and risk the breach?

steps.symptom: CVE lands with a 9.8 score and a public exploit. The vulnerable service faces the internet. The launch freeze started yesterday.
evidence: Advisory

CVE-2026-44112 | CVSS 9.8 | RCE | public exploit published
Affected: public-facing API gateway (1 host)
Change freeze: in effect until launch, tomorrow 09:00
options: Patch immediately — freeze or no freeze
First verify actual exposure: is the vulnerable code path reachable, is there a compensating control?
Hold the patch until after the launch
Take the API gateway offline until the launch is over
steps.explain: A 9.8 with a public exploit demands urgency, not panic. Verify exposure first: an unreachable code path or a WAF rule in front of it changes the math completely. You cannot make the patch-vs-launch call without knowing the real risk.

steps.symptom: Exposure confirmed: the vulnerable endpoint is reachable, no WAF in front of it. Scans from the internet started 20 minutes ago.
evidence: Telemetry

Vulnerable endpoint: reachable from internet
Inbound scanning for the exploit signature: started 20 min ago
No WAF or compensating control in path
options: Declare an emergency change, patch now, accept the launch risk
Wait for the vendor's official patch next week
Block the exploit signature at the edge as a stopgap and patch in the emergency window tonight
Hope the scanners are just researchers
steps.explain: Both risks are real, so you sequence them: a signature block at the edge buys hours (imperfect but immediate), and the real patch lands in tonight's emergency window. 'Patch now and break the launch' and 'hold and get breached' are both failure modes — the stopgap is the third option.

steps.symptom: The launch team demands a plain-English answer: why are you touching production during the freeze?
evidence: Ask
Launch lead: 'Explain to me like I am the CEO: why does this override the freeze?'
options: Quote the CVSS score and the CVE number
'Attackers are scanning us right now for a flaw that lets them run code on our gateway. We put a shield up and we patch tonight — the launch is protected, not threatened.'
Refuse to explain — security decisions are not debatable
Promise the launch will be unaffected
steps.explain: Risk translated into business language: who is attacking, what they get, what you did, what happens next. CVSS numbers do not move executives; 'they can run code on our front door and we are handling it tonight' does.

simulations.debrief: You verified exposure before choosing, sequenced a stopgap ahead of the real fix, and translated the risk into language the business could act on. That is vulnerability management under pressure.

simulations.title: The vendor wants the keys
simulations.brief: A new analytics vendor wants production database access with a shared service account and no expiry. The contract is signed; the business wants the dashboards live this week. Decide the access model.

steps.symptom: The vendor's onboarding doc asks for: a production DB login, shared service account, full read on all tables, no expiry.
evidence: Vendor request

Access: production database, all tables, read
Account: single shared 'vendor_svc' login
Expiry: none requested | MFA: not supported by their tooling
options: Grant it as requested — the contract is signed and the business is waiting
Offer a read replica with a scoped, named, expiring service account and IP allowlisting
Deny all access and kill the project
Give them the credentials over a screen share so at least it is not in email
steps.explain: Least privilege is a negotiation, not a veto: a read replica (never production), a named account (attribution), an expiry (no forever-keys), and IP allowlisting (their office, not the internet). The dashboards still go live this week — on your terms.

steps.symptom: The vendor pushes back: 'Our tool needs production. The replica lags too much for real-time dashboards.'
evidence: Pushback
Vendor: 'Replica lag is 30 seconds. Our SLA needs under 5.'
options: Cave and grant production access
Measure the actual requirement: is any business decision made on sub-5-second data? Offer a scoped production read on the two needed tables, query-audited
Tell them to rebuild their tool
Ignore the pushback and hope they adapt
steps.explain: Challenge the requirement with data: almost no dashboard decision needs 5-second freshness, but if it genuinely does, you narrow production access to the two tables that need it — with every query logged. Scope follows proven need, not asserted need.

steps.symptom: Access is agreed. Now protect the relationship long-term.
evidence: Ongoing
Vendor account will exist for the life of the contract
options: Set a 90-day expiry with a renewal review, alert on anomalous query volume, and document the access in the vendor risk register
Set it and forget it
Rotate the password every day to be safe
Ask the vendor to self-attest annually
steps.explain: Third-party access rots: people leave, contracts change, tools get breached. Expiry forces a review, anomaly alerts catch abuse, and the risk register means the next person inherits the context instead of discovering a mystery account.

simulations.debrief: You negotiated least privilege instead of issuing a veto, tested the vendor's real requirements, and built expiry and monitoring into the relationship. Vendor risk management is access design, not access denial.

consoleSims.title: Default-deny the lab workstation
consoleSims.brief: A new lab workstation joins the fleet. Policy is deny-by-default: set the INPUT chain default to DROP, then open exactly one hole — HTTPS (TCP 443) from the corporate network 10.0.0.0/8.

tasks.instruction: Add an ACCEPT rule: chain INPUT, TCP port 443, source 10.0.0.0/8.
tasks.hint: Use the Add rule form: CHAIN=INPUT, PROTOCOL=tcp, PORT=443, SOURCE=10.0.0.0/8, ACTION=ACCEPT.

tasks.instruction: Set the INPUT chain default policy to DROP.
tasks.hint: Open Default policies and set INPUT to DROP — everything not explicitly allowed must fall through to deny.

consoleSims.debrief: One explicit allow, everything else denied. That is deny-by-default in its purest form: the policy says what may happen, and silence means no.

consoleSims.title: SSH only from the admin net
consoleSims.brief: Audit found SSH open to the world on a jump host. Lock it down: allow TCP 22 only from the admin network 192.168.50.0/24, then set the INPUT default policy to DROP so the old wide-open posture cannot return.

tasks.instruction: Add an ACCEPT rule: chain INPUT, TCP port 22, source 192.168.50.0/24.
tasks.hint: Add rule form: CHAIN=INPUT, PROTOCOL=tcp, PORT=22, SOURCE=192.168.50.0/24, ACTION=ACCEPT.

tasks.instruction: Set the INPUT chain default policy to DROP.
tasks.hint: Under Default policies, set INPUT to DROP. The old allow-from-anywhere posture dies with the default.

consoleSims.debrief: Management-plane services get the smallest possible audience. SSH from one admin network, deny by default — the internet never needs your jump host.

consoleSims.title: Work the alert queue
consoleSims.brief: Three alerts are sitting open, oldest first. Triage like an analyst: acknowledge the critical malware-hash alert ALT-102, assign it to analyst 'r.okafor', then escalate it to incident response.

tasks.hint: In the Alerts table, click Ack on the ALT-102 row (Malware hash match on download).

tasks.instruction: Assign alert ALT-102 to analyst r.okafor.
tasks.hint: Use the Assign alert form: ALERT ID=ALT-102, ANALYST=r.okafor.

tasks.instruction: Escalate alert ALT-102 to incident response.
tasks.hint: Click Escalate on the ALT-102 row — a critical malware match does not sit in the queue.

consoleSims.debrief: Acknowledge, assign, escalate: the alert is owned, worked, and moved to the team that can contain it. Queues do not clear themselves.

consoleSims.title: Contain and detect
consoleSims.brief: ALT-103 shows unusual outbound volume from srv-backup-02 — possible exfiltration. Isolate the host now, then write a detection rule so the next one fires faster.

tasks.hint: Click 'Isolate host' on the ALT-103 row — stop the bleeding before you analyze it.

tasks.instruction: Create a detection rule named 'outbound-volume-spike' with a query matching unusual outbound volume.
tasks.hint: Open Detection rules and create a rule: NAME=outbound-volume-spike, QUERY describing unusual outbound bytes (any descriptive query text works).

consoleSims.debrief: Contain first, detect forever after. Every real incident should leave a detection rule behind — that is how a SOC gets smarter instead of just busier.

terminalMissions.title: Identify yourself to the SOC
terminalMissions.brief: Every incident starts with identity. Print your username — the SOC needs to know who is on the keyboard.

checks.hint: Run: whoami — who is operating this station?

terminalMissions.success_message: Identity confirmed: candidate. Attribution starts with knowing who acted.

terminalMissions.title: Confirm your station
terminalMissions.brief: Verify which machine you are on. Print the hostname — incident reports must name the host.

checks.hint: Run: echo with a confirmation naming your station (e.g. echo "on station interstitium").

terminalMissions.success_message: Station confirmed. Reports name the host, always.

terminalMissions.title: Inventory the workstation
terminalMissions.brief: Before you touch anything, know what is here. List the home directory.

checks.hint: Run: ls — inventory the workstation. What study material is here?

terminalMissions.success_message: Workstation inventoried. Situational awareness before action — always.

terminalMissions.title: Declare the incident
terminalMissions.brief: A phishing report just landed. Declare it on the channel with echo — declarations must be explicit and visible, never assumed.

checks.hint: Run: echo with an incident declaration (e.g. echo "SECURITY INCIDENT DECLARED").

terminalMissions.success_message: Incident declared. If nobody says it, nobody owns it.

terminalMissions.title: Verify your identity token
terminalMissions.brief: Access reviews check the full identity string, not just the name. Print your identity record.

checks.hint: Run: id — read the full identity string.

terminalMissions.success_message: Identity verified: uid=1000. Reviews check the whole record, not the username.

terminalMissions.title: Check the platform build
terminalMissions.brief: Know your platform: print the full system information. Vulnerability management starts with knowing what you run.

checks.hint: Run: uname -a — read the platform build string.

terminalMissions.success_message: Platform identified. You cannot protect what you cannot name.

terminalMissions.title: Confirm your operating position
terminalMissions.brief: Print your working directory, then attest with echo that your position is confirmed — two independent confirmations, like any good control.

checks.hint: Run: pwd — where are you operating from?
Run: echo with a confirmation (e.g. echo "position confirmed").

terminalMissions.success_message: Position confirmed twice. Defense in depth applies to verification too.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it

items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.alt: A policy engine at the center of a small graph evaluates an access request from a finance user on an untrusted laptop to an R and D code server. The request is denied because there is no prior relationship edge and the device is untrusted.
media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.
media.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
media.caption: UEBA learns each user's normal hours, locations, and volumes, then scores deviations from that baseline.
media.alt: 24-hour timeline showing a shaded normal login window from 8 AM to 6 PM with normal logins inside it, and a red anomaly marker at 2:47 AM for a foreign login scoring 97 out of 100.

media.title: Indirect prompt injection attack flow
media.caption: An attacker hides instructions in data the agent retrieves; the agent mistakes data for instructions and misuses its tools.
media.alt: Attack flow diagram: hidden instruction in an email is read by an AI agent, which mistakes it for a command and calls a privileged tool, causing fraud; three defense boxes below: sanitize content, least-privilege tools, human approval.
